opus-5.5.text:
I think the key thing to recognize is that the problem isn't really about *how* you generate the image. It's about *what you're asking the model to predict* in the first place.

When we train on interleaved image-text data scraped from the web, like articles, tutorials, or blog posts with pictures, the natural move is to treat it like text: given everything before, predict what comes next. For text tokens, that works reasonably well. But when the next thing is an image, the preceding context almost never actually determines that image. Someone writes a paragraph about their trip to Kyoto and then inserts a photo. Which photo? Taken from which angle, with what lighting, what composition? The text constrains it a little, but the vast majority of the pixel-level information in that image is essentially random relative to the context. It's high-entropy content the model has no way of inferring.

So if you force the model to predict that image, you're giving it a supervision signal that is mostly noise. Worse than noise, really, because the model will try to fit it. It learns to hallucinate spurious correlations, or it pours capacity into modeling low-level texture statistics that have nothing to do with understanding or reasoning. That's what I mean by harmful supervision. It doesn't just fail to help; it can actively hurt the model's other capabilities.

Now, some people hoped autoregressive image generation would fix this. The idea is that if you tokenize images into discrete tokens and predict them one by one just like text, you get a unified framework and everything scales the same way. It's elegant, but it doesn't touch the root cause. Whether you predict the image with diffusion, with continuous regression, or with discrete next-token prediction, you're still asking the model to produce something the context doesn't determine. Changing the decoder doesn't change the information-theoretic fact that the target is underdetermined.

In some ways autoregressive generation makes it more visible. An image becomes hundreds or thousands of tokens, so in the loss the image part can easily dominate the text part. Most of those tokens encode local detail: edges, textures, color patches. So the gradient is overwhelmingly spent on "make the pixels plausible" rather than "understand what's going on." You've converted the semantic problem into a massive low-level prediction problem and then weighted it heavily.

There's also a tokenizer issue. Discrete visual tokenizers are mostly trained for reconstruction, so their tokens carry a lot of appearance information and relatively little semantic structure. Predicting them pulls the model toward pixel statistics, not concepts. That's quite different from language, where tokens are already highly compressed, human-designed semantic units. Text has been "pre-abstracted" by humans; images haven't.

So my view is that the real fix has to be at the level of the training objective and the data, not the generation architecture. You have to ask: for this image, in this context, what part is actually predictable? Maybe it's the high-level semantics, like "there's a temple, it's autumn." Maybe the image should be treated purely as a conditioning input rather than a prediction target. Or you need data where the image genuinely follows causally from the text, like editing instructions, step-by-step diagrams, or rendered results of a described process. Only there is the supervision clean.

Autoregression gives you a unified interface, which is nice from an engineering standpoint. But a unified interface isn't the same as a correct objective. If the target is fundamentally unpredictable, no tokenization scheme can make that supervision healthy.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer directly as the guest.

I think the core of the problem is this: when you do interleaved image-text training, the hope is that the text and the images will teach each other. The text should help you understand the image, and the image should help you predict the text. But in practice, the gradient flowing back from the image tokens is often not helpful for the language model at all. It's harmful.

Why? Because an image carries an enormous amount of information, and most of that information is low-level: textures, lighting, the exact position of pixels, noise. When you force the model to predict image tokens autoregressively, you are asking it to spend capacity on modeling that low-level detail. That signal has almost nothing to do with semantics, with reasoning, with the things that make a language model intelligent. So you get a model that is pulled in two directions: one part wants to compress semantics, the other part is being pushed to memorize pixel statistics.

People sometimes think switching to autoregressive image generation fixes this, because now everything is one unified next-token prediction objective. The form looks clean. But the content of the supervision hasn't changed. You've just tokenized the pixels and put them in a sequence. The loss on those tokens is still dominated by low-level reconstruction. Whether you call it diffusion loss or cross-entropy over VQ tokens, the model is still being supervised to reproduce information that is irrelevant or even harmful to understanding.

There's also an asymmetry that autoregression doesn't resolve. Text is already a highly compressed, human-filtered representation. Images are raw. If you treat them symmetrically in the same sequence, the raw modality dominates the loss simply by volume. One image might be hundreds or thousands of tokens, and a caption might be twenty. So the optimization is quietly tilted toward generation, and the understanding side pays for it.

My view is that the real fix has to be about what you supervise, not how you order the tokens. You need a representation of the image where the supervision target is already semantic, where predicting it forces the model to understand rather than reconstruct. Only then does interleaved training become a two-way street where image tokens actually help the language side instead of hurting it. Autoregression is a nice unifying interface, but it's an interface, not a solution.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between how you generate an image and what you ask the model to learn. Autoregressive generation changes the factorization—you predict image tokens one at a time—but it doesn’t automatically fix the supervision coming from interleaved image and text.

For example, text accompanying an image might describe only one aspect of it. If you train the model to predict every image token from that text, you’re also asking it to predict lots of details that the text never specified. Those details may be legitimate targets for visual modeling, but they aren’t necessarily useful supervision for learning the relationship between language and vision. And if the text and image are poorly aligned, making the image prediction autoregressive doesn’t remove that mismatch.

So I wouldn’t say autoregression is inherently harmful. I’d say it doesn’t, by itself, distinguish useful cross-modal supervision from irrelevant or misleading prediction targets. You still have to address the data alignment and the training objective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between changing the generation objective and changing the supervision itself. Autoregressive image generation changes how we predict an image, but it doesn’t necessarily change what the interleaved image-text sequence asks the model to learn.

For example, text placed next to an image may describe only a small part of it, or may be loosely related to it. If we train the model to predict that text conditioned on the image, we can still push it to learn associations that aren’t visually grounded. Making the image tokens autoregressive doesn’t remove that mismatch.

So it may give us a more unified architecture and a richer training signal, but it isn’t a fundamental solution to harmful supervision. We still need to consider which relationships in the sequence are reliable enough to supervise, and which prediction targets actually encourage visual understanding.
